text:
Established HPO benchmarking uses anytime incumbent curves: best validation score available versus cumulative computation, alongside final performance at a fixed budget. Random search is a standard comparator ([Bergstra–Bengio](https://jmlr.org/papers/v13/bergstra12a.html)); benchmarking guidance recommends whole optimization traces and explicit optimizer overhead ([Bischl et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.05847)). Applied here: compare diagnostic guidance, random search over identical configuration distributions, and a prespecified strong SASRec baseline. Charge training, diagnostics, validation, debugging and failures against equal GPU-second budgets; report CPU/LLM overhead separately. With concurrent trials, sum GPU consumption across workers and publish wall-clock time separately. Plot macro validation HR@10 against cost; summarize endpoint scores and optionally area under the incumbent curve.

Predeclare deadline handling: charge unfinished trials their consumed resources, but update incumbents only from eligible evaluations available before cutoff. Carry the previous incumbent forward; never backfill a late result. Runtime censoring has established treatment in [Hutter et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.1947), but an unfinished trial’s final HR@10 is missing—not a known upper or lower bound. To isolate guidance, repeat entire adaptive searches with different search seeds while fixing preprocessing/training/evaluation seeds at 0/42/42. Match initialization, worker count and stopping rules; report paired differences and uncertainty across searches. These repetitions quantify search randomness, not training-seed robustness.

Repeated validation selection creates optimism even with fixed seeds; more adaptive queries can exploit validation noise ([Cawley–Talbot](https://www.jmlr.org/beta/papers/v11/cawley10a.html)). Freeze methods and selection rules before independent held-out evaluation. Under pinned splits, retain validation curves as search outcomes and reserve hidden-test evaluation for the frozen final selection. Search-seed repetitions do not remove validation-selection bias.
